title: Risk-Calibrated Escalation for Multi-Agent Workflows
research_question: Can a multi-agent workflow controller that explicitly models model-selection uncertainty and escalates only high-ambiguity subproblems to additional agents or verification steps improve task success per unit cost versus fixed orchestration policies?
hypothesis: Because existing adaptive-system evidence shows that selecting a single best model can produce overconfident decisions, a workflow controller that maintains multiple plausible execution hypotheses and escalates only when posterior uncertainty remains high will reduce unnecessary adaptations while improving reliability in agentic task decomposition and orchestration.
motivation: The knowledge base highlights an open uncertainty gap: Bayesian model averaging has been shown useful for self-adaptive systems because single-model decisions can be overconfident and trigger missed or unnecessary adaptations, yet the adjacent agentic-workflow space already contains rejected ideas around generic Bayesian orchestration and bandit verifier allocation. This suggests a narrower, more novel angle: not broad uncertainty-aware orchestration, but risk-calibrated escalation at the subproblem level for task decomposition, where the controller tracks multiple plausible execution states and invokes extra critique, retrieval, or verification only when ambiguity is unresolved. That targets the high-priority agentic-workflow-optimization direction while avoiding direct overlap with previously rejected broad proposals.
